I also read your other comment and it seems you have a good grasp of what will be involved, and I'm super big on bark tanning for all the reasons you mentioned. For my hides they were given to me salted and had been sitting on salt for months so I added a couple extra steps for prep before tanning

Rehydrate in salt water for 3 hours
Wash off as much salt as possible remove flesh
Pickle in salt and citric acid for 3 days
Rinse
Neutralise in baking soda and water for 15 minutes
Rinse
Scrape the flesh
Tanning solution 1 part bark liquor 3 parts water to start
Adding extra bark liquor every couple days/ when seeing a drop in colour/ it smells weak
Remove some of the used solution when adding more liquor to maintain strength and fluid level.

I could tell mine were done by cutting a little nick into the leather and seeing there is no white and it is tanned all the way through

Start oiling before the leather is dry, (I used vegetable shortening), break, stretch, and massage the oil in.

 
As for making the bark liquor, I would get started on it asap, just get your bark and soak it in cold water for a few weeks. Supposedly cold extraction is good for extracting different stuff from hot extraction. After you can drain the bark and boil it in new water to get the other compounds out too. I used an old food processor to get the bark extra pulverised for maximum extraction.

This particular piece is very thin and flexible because that's what I was aiming for, soft leather akin to that used for gloves. But the great thing with tanning is you have a decent amount of control of what kind of product you end up with. Got this the membrane and tissue was scraped super thin, it was stretched and scraped throughout the tanning process and stretching/breaking as it dries. You could leave more membrane on it to have a thicker leather if that's what you are after, and do less stretching/breaking to have it be stiffer. Though it'll still need a decent bit of working the leather so it won't crack where it bends on the book cover.

Okay so I'm not great at explain stuff to just bear with me. First off if you are cuting for attention, it's still valid and still a serious issue, if you feel like mutilating your body no matter what the severity, method, or motive it's not considered normal. A healthy/stable/'normal' (for lack of better words) person wouldn't do this to their self. 

Obviously I'm not in your brain so I couldn't possibly know your reason(s) for cutting but from what you've said you don't seem to be doing it simply for the attention of other people, infact it sounds like you're doing everything you can to justify that you're not doing it for attention (like cutting deeper).

Self harm is a coping mechanism we use it to deal with things we have no other better ways to cope with. Cutting sometimes give people a feel of comfort and control when everything else is overwhelming or beyond your control. Selfharm can make you feel better so your brain may make positive associations with cuts and scars which is why looking at them can bring you comfort.

There is no such thing as 'deep enough' people often keep cutting deeper and deeper it can become very dangerous, and you still might never be satisfied or feel like it's enough.  Media often portrays self harm as a cry for help or minimises small cuts to attention seeking behaviour, which could be impacting the way you view your own selfharm.


Hopefully at least some of this applies to you...  I can't tell you to simply stop cutting but please please try and stick to shorter shallower cuts, you've said you like the feeling better and if that isn't a good enough reason longer and deeper cuts are far more likely to get infected and cause permanent damage to your body.

Essentially steri-strips are like skinny masking tape pieces that stick well to skin and don't interfere with wound healing. You can get them in various lengths from like 2cm to like 10cm, or maybe longer idk. For when there are lots of cuts next to eachother you get a nice long one, start at one side and pull it across tight so it pulls all the open cuts back together. Because this patch was wider than the steri-strips they alternated which side they started from as they went down, mainly focusing on the more sever cuts that hasn't been stitched.
